chapter_theme: The king refuses to kill a kid, is pressed into striking a flour cock, which cries out; the queen, pretending to join his renunciation, poisons him and his mother, and the mourners and the teller read the deaths by deeds.

cast.role: the king, named Yasodharan at verse 149; the queen's husband
the king's queen, who poisons him and his mother
the king's mother, who counsels the flour-cock offering
the king's son, crowned at verse 159
the king's attendants and the townspeople who judge him and the queen
the teller who relates the tale to Maridattan
the king to whom the tale is told

140.reading: The king tells his mother that to kill the weak so that he may live would turn him from the road to heaven, and that a human life ends in death on the earth in any case.
140.nuance: The verse carries on the refusal begun at 138-139 and adds its reasons: the cost in the next world, and the shortness of this one.
140.event: The king gives his mother his reason for refusing to kill a creature to save himself.

claims.claim: killing the weak to preserve one's own life turns the killer from the way to heaven
a human life ends in death on earth whatever is done to keep it

141.reading: Addressing his mother, the king says her family never did cruel killing, and that if the sin of killing a life brings many sorrows today, all she has urged is no kindness to him.
141.nuance: He turns his mother's care against her counsel: what she calls help would be harm to him.
141.event: The king appeals to his family's past and to the sorrow that killing breeds.

claims.claim: the sin of killing a life ripens in many sorrows

142.reading: Angered that he has defied her, the mother calls him cruel, then offers another way: if he fears taking a life, let him make a cock of flour, offer it as a sacrifice and please the goddess.
142.nuance: The proposal is a loophole in the king's refusal, offered in the same breath as her anger.
142.event: The mother proposes a flour cock as a substitute for a living offering.

claims.claim: a sacrifice made with an image of a living creature can please the goddess and ward off the dream's evil

143.reading: The king, in a verse whose first half is hard, sets the queen's false dream-tale against his mother's counsel and says that, with his deeds now rising and many sorrows come upon him, no one can keep the ripening of deeds away.
143.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard (the sense of the queen's 'dream-tale' set against 'the goddess's counsel'). The reading of the first half is provisional; the king's words in lines 3 and 4 are clear.
143.event: The king, standing before his mother, says that no one can turn back what his deeds are ripening.

claims.claim: no one can ward off the ripening of deeds

144.reading: Although the king shrinks even from making the shape of a living creature, as it is like killing, he is not firm enough to cut his ties, and so consents to do what his mother angrily told him.
144.nuance: The last line is hard (அயிர்ப்பதென் அறத்தின் திண்மை). The reading takes it as the narrator's remark that his hold on dharma was not firm enough to be sure.
144.event: The king agrees, against his own misgiving, to the flour-cock offering.

claims.claim: making the likeness of a living creature is felt to be like killing

145.reading: The king takes the flour-made cock with his mother to the goddess's place of slaughter, bows with honour and cuts it with his own sword, saying that it was offered to her.
145.nuance: The place is called the place of killing (படுகொலைக்கிடம்); the king goes not as the sacrificer's helper but as the one who strikes.
145.event: The king beheads the flour cock before the goddess with his own sword.

146.reading: The goddess is pleased, and the flour cock, its head cut, runs before the king crying, shakes and falls, so that the king drops his sword and is moved with pity.
146.nuance: The narrator treats the flour bird as a creature that cries out; the work thereby answers the mother's claim that a likeness is a harmless substitute.
146.event: The flour cock cries and falls when the king's sword strikes it, and the king drops the sword.

147.reading: The king asks what has happened to the flour cock that received life, why it ran and cried under his sword, and whether the sin that brings the chain of births its great fault is calling him.
147.nuance: The fear is put as a question; the deaths at 153 are the poem's later answer.
147.event: The king questions the living cry of the flour cock and fears the sin has come to him.

claims.claim: killing, even of a made likeness, brings a sin that binds to a chain of births

148.reading: In regret, the king cries out that he did a graceless thing by his mother's words, that the cry of the bird tears his heart, and that his deeds may now stand over him and crush him.
148.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are obscure (the repeated ஆதகா and a clause about the 'nectar' lady); the reading rests on lines 1 and 4.
148.event: The king laments the graceless act and fears his deeds.

claims.claim: a deed done without grace returns on the doer as ripened deeds

149.reading: Thinking so, Yasodharan goes back to the city, sets his son on the throne and sets out for the forest of austerity; the queen, knowing it and thinking that he spurned her, does something that will send her to the burning hell.
149.nuance: The narrator names the queen's end before her act, so the poison that follows is told as already judged.
149.event: The king hands the kingdom to his son and leaves for the ascetic forest, and the queen resents it.

claims.claim: the queen who acts on her hurt will fall into burning hell

150.reading: The queen tells the king that if he gives up the kingdom, so will she; she begs him to come to her house that day with his son and take the sweet drink, and let the kingdom be the son's while they become ascetics.
150.nuance: The speech is a pretence, as 152 says (வஞ்சனை வலித்து): her renunciation is the bait.
150.event: The queen feigns agreement with the king's renunciation and invites him to her house.

151.reading: Though the king knows what lies in her heart, he tells her to do as she wishes and, bearing his mother with him, goes to sit in her house; the verse adds that when ruin is near even a wrong course seems the right one.
151.nuance: Line 1 can be read as the king's knowledge of her intent or of her worth; the reading takes the first.
151.event: The king, knowing her mind, goes with his mother to the queen's house.

claims.claim: when ruin draws near, a wrong course appears right counsel

152.reading: The queen mixes poison with honey and sweet food, gives it to her husband and his mother as a dish for both, and takes the unpoisoned part herself with her son.
152.nuance: The honey's sweetness hides the poison: the same sweetness the Kural praises in speech here covers murder.
152.event: The queen serves poisoned food to the king and his mother.

153.reading: As the poison spreads they tremble and fall in a swoon, fear death, and the deeds they had heaped come in; the senses fail and they die, to fall into the animal state that knows no end of pain.
153.nuance: Both are given as causes: the queen's poison is the means, and the ripening of the family's own deeds is the narrator's reason. The poem does not say that the woman's act is excused by karma.
153.event: The king and his mother die of the poison and are reborn among animals.

claims.claim: heaped deeds ripen at death and send the dying into animal births

154.reading: The mourners say that this queen, unfit even for counting, thought of a low man unfit for eyes to see, killed her husband the lord of lands, and is the most wrathful and sinful of women.
154.nuance: This is the people's judgment in their own grief, not the narrator's; the narrator has already judged her at 149.
154.event: The mourners condemn the queen who killed her husband for a base lover.

claims.claim: a wife who kills her husband for a base lover is the greatest sinner among women

155.reading: Some of the mourners say that the king made an image of a god free of evil, yet, though he saw the world's wishes fulfilled before such an image, threw a living-shaped offering to the goddess without discernment, and so this has come today.
155.nuance: The mourners join the offering at 145 to the poison; the poem gives the same link in the narrator's voice at 153 only as ripened deeds, not as this one offering.
155.event: Some mourners trace the king's death to his flour-cock offering.

claims.claim: offering even the likeness of a living creature to a deity brings its fruit upon the offerer

156.reading: Others say that the king did not enjoy the wealth of dharma, was not easy for the great ascetics to reach, and was deluded by wrong things and joyful in rule; he died young while others were stingy with pleasure, and no good death waits at the end, so what is his destination?
156.nuance: The mourners judge the king by his rule alone; the narrator's account of his refusal to kill at 138 to 140 shows what they cannot see.
156.event: The mourners doubt the king's destination.

claims.claim: one who delights in rule and does not take up dharma has no good death and an uncertain next birth

157.reading: The attendants and the townspeople weep at these thoughts, while the queen, who has done what she wished, her mind weakened by the strain, calls her son.
157.event: The people mourn while the queen calls her son.

158.reading: The queen tells her son that he is alone now, that the loss of the king came from the fruit of her own deeds, bids him leave off the heart's sorrow, wear the crown and rule the earth, and sits glad, the nectar of her secret lord.
158.nuance: The queen speaks the poem's own doctrine of karma to hide a deed that is hers; the poem uses the same words to expose her.
158.event: The queen consoles her son and bids him rule.

claims.claim: the loss of her husband came from the ripening of her own deeds

159.reading: With the drums beating, Yasomati puts on the jewelled crown and takes up lordship; he does not turn to the teacher's gift of dharma but sinks into a sea of the delight of women.
159.event: Yasomati is crowned and gives himself to pleasure.

160.reading: The teller says to Maridattan that if he understands that such things arise from deeds, these will be his companions and from them joy will grow, while those without that clarity only rule the earth and wear the flowered crown.
160.nuance: The speaker is taken to be the teller of the tale to the king Maridattan, from the frame laid in the second chapter; the verse itself names only the addressee.
160.event: Sudattan draws the lesson of the king's death for Maridattan.

claims.claim: outcomes arise from deeds, and one who understands this gains true companions and joy

links.note: The king refuses to kill even to save his own life, and gives the cost in the next world and the shortness of this one.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the rule alone; the king adds the reason that makes it bear on a man whose own life is threatened.

gains.a: The king's refusal is shown to rest on a known maxim, not only on his temper.
gains.b: The couplet gets a man whose own life is truly threatened and who must pay for obeying it.

links.note: After the king says no life may be taken, his mother offers a flour cock in the same breath.
links.teaches: Placing the loophole next to the refusal shows the poem is testing whether a made likeness of life counts as a life.

links.note: The king says no one can turn back the ripening of deeds, then agrees to the rite meant to ward off the dream's evil.
links.teaches: The king's own words deny the rite he accepts, which shows his consent as weakness, not belief.

links.note: The king asks who can turn aside the ripening of deeds.
links.teaches: The couplet says fate outruns any other device; the king acts that out, trying the mother's device and finding the fruit still comes.

gains.a: The king's question gets an authority that answers it before the story does.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where a device is tried and fate comes first.

links.note: The king consents to the flour-cock offering his mother proposes.
links.teaches: His doubt in 144 shows the loophole of 142 does not satisfy even the one who takes it, which prepares the cry at 146.

links.note: The flour cock cries and falls under the sword, answering the king's fear that a likeness is like killing.
links.teaches: The king's disgust at a likeness of life in 144 is borne out by the cry at 146, which shows his instinct was sound against his mother's argument.

links.note: The goddess's slaughter-place recurs, once for the two youths and now for a flour cock struck by the king.
links.teaches: The same altar shows the poem's shift: from killing living victims to a substitute that still cries out, so the question is not only the victim but the act.

links.note: The king asks what the cry of the flour cock means and fears the sin.
links.teaches: His question turns the marvel at 146 into doctrine: the cry is read as the sign of a sin that binds to births.

links.note: The king's wish to give up the kingdom was real; the queen offers the same renunciation as bait.
links.teaches: The poem sets sincere and false renunciation in the same words, so the reader sees renunciation can be counterfeited by one who means murder.

links.note: The king and his mother enter the animal state at death, and the youth at 34 tells of wandering among animals and being killed by kin.
links.teaches: The animal birth at 153 is the state whose pains are told later in the youth's account, so the ripening is followed across births.

links.note: Hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself, as the king's offering returns on him through the poison.
links.teaches: The couplet says the hurt returns of itself; 153 shows it returning through a third person's crime, so the doer suffers without being punished by the doer's own victim.

gains.a: The poison is seen as the late fruit of an earlier act of harm.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where the returning hurt comes through another's crime, not the victim's hand.

links.note: A deed that seeks out the one who did it, like a calf finding its mother in a herd.
links.teaches: The quatrain's image says deeds find their doer; 153 shows how: they come in at the hour of the poison and ripen into animal births.

gains.a: The deeds that 'came in' are given an image of seeking the doer out.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a death in which the deed ripens by an unrelated hand.

links.note: The king had judged that women are not fit to be killed and spared the queen.
links.teaches: His mercy at 124 is read here as the cause of his death, so the poem asks whether sparing the guilty was a fault or a virtue.

links.note: The mourners link the king's death to the flour cock he struck.
links.teaches: The mourners trace the poison back to the offering at 145, a reading the narrator does not himself make.

links.note: The mourners say he took no part in dharma and has no good death; the king had refused to kill even to save his own life.
links.teaches: The mourners judge by what they saw, but 139 shows the refusal that belongs to the king's dharma, so their verdict is incomplete.

links.note: The king says no one can turn the ripening of deeds from him; the queen uses the same words to excuse her own deed.
links.teaches: The same doctrine from a victim and from the poisoner shows karma can be spoken as comfort or as an excuse.

links.note: The poem opens by saying it will show how deeds ripen, and the teller here draws that lesson for Maridattan.
links.teaches: The closing lesson at 160 answers the promise at 4, so the reader is told that the whole tale was an argument about deeds.

links.note: The teller says that understanding that events arise from deeds gives true companions and joy; the Siddhar says the body is the enjoyment of deeds and joins those who think of Siva's feet.
links.teaches: The epic makes understanding the nature of deeds the first step; the Siddhar names grace at the feet as what takes one beyond them.

gains.a: The epic's lesson meets the Saiva claim that a god's feet, not understanding, release one from deeds.
gains.b: The Siddhar's body-as-deeds gets a long case in which deeds ripen through poison and rebirth.

new_concepts.gloss: an offering, especially of a life, made to a deity

source_issues: Verses 143, 144, 148 and 155 have obscure lines; the readings are provisional.
Verse 160's speaker is inferred from the story's frame.
